doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Improv workbook and chord scales at Berklee
summary: He teaches improvisation starting from chords and scales with his own workbook and recalls Phil Woods joking about 2-5-1.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Do you have a way to set these students up when you start teaching them improvisation so that it will be likely that they will play something they’re comfortable with?

Down the hall I used to teach a lab for improv, beginning and intermediate levels, two different, maybe eight or ten students, woodwind students, flute, you know, sax, clarinet, even a bassoon once. I had to re-write some music in bass clef. And you know to get someone that can even play a little bebop is crazy [scats] it’s like no one could do that. It’s rare you know. But anyway, but I have about a fifteen page, or thirty page improv workbook that I wrote for Berklee. And like I tell the students the first lesson, “There’s about ten or fifteen good teachers here, like myself, or players like myself, and each person has their own way to present jazz to you. I start with chords and scales you know. That’s basic in music. Some people might just do blues. I’m not teaching just by ear. That’s not my thing. And I’ve had some students in ensembles that have real good ears and play good, so I don’t think I have too much to teach them because they’re naturally talented. Not everybody is with a good ear. But I have this book. So I start with chords. The first page is all the seven or eight different types of chords you see in the fake book or Real Book, standard tunes; major seventh, diminished, whatever. In the key of C and it’s just demonstrated with the tension notes, the ninths, elevenths, thirteenths. Chord tones and tensions. And then on the right side of the page I have the chord scales that they teach at Berklee. I think Phil Woods years ago did a clinic, no he was playing a performance with Hal Crook, one of the great trombone players, teaches here. And I laughed. He was playing acoustically first of all, in a big auditorium that holds a thousand people. And he says, “You know, kids, it’s not all 2-5-1.” And I thought that was very cute and funny. Because jazz tunes have 2-5s in them you know. And he didn’t go into that chord scales. But in those days they had a tee shirt in black and white that had all 2-5 progressions, front and back you know. But I didn’t learn chord scales. It was funny I told some students years ago, I was walking down the street from one building to the next to teach. And a teacher, a piano player, I think it was Mike — I don’t want to get the name wrong, so, I don’t know if he’s still here. He’s a little older than me. But he went to Berklee when I did, in 1961.
